title: The New Industrialists | Autonomous Pipeline Optimization: Industrial Automation in Oil & Gas
transcriptText:
(upbeat music)
- Welcome to The New Industrialists.
I'm here today with Adam
Marsden, CRO of CRUXOCM.
Adam, it's great to have you on a show.
- Thank you for having me.
- Could you please tell us a
little bit about your company?
- Of course.
So, just like how autopilot
is available on airplanes
for the last five or six decades,
what my company has
developed is a framework
that allows for closed loop control
to autonomously execute
real-time commands for pipeline
and other assets in the oil and gas space.
What this allows us to do is ultimately
to get increased throughput,
up to seven percent,
reduced energy costs up to 10%,
as well as increasing asset lifespan
and reliability of your pipeline assets.
- This close loop autonomy,
that's been a dream
in the industry for many years.
Like, is it becoming real now?
- Yes.
So specifically what we're doing is,
for midstream, in oil
and gas, that's an area
that closed loop autonomy has
never really graced before.
So we've taken it from other
places such as downstream
or other industries,
we've applied the patents
and now we're actually facilitating it
real time in pipelines.
So it's something that
they've been trying to do for,
you know, 15, 20 years,
they hook up simulators
and that sort of stuff,
but unfortunately, simulators don't have
the AI capabilities or
really just the compute power
to do it quick enough,
so using the closed loop mechanisms
that we have at our disposal now,
we're able to perform that
and do it on behalf of folks.
- When I talk to customers,
there was always this disbelief
every time I bring close loop
and because basically it's
autonomy, some level of autonomy.
Can you really do it?
- Yeah.
So one of the hardest things that we do
with any customers, at least initially,
is getting in and getting them past that
initial barrier of, oh my gosh,
like A, like, can you do this?
And now that we're past
that A, can we do that,
it's B like, can we do this safely?
And especially with all
the tools at our disposal,
like, are you able to
perform this as safe as--
- Is safety what matters or
is it, can you do it at scale?
- So both.
So especially in our
industry in oil and gas,
they go hand in hand.
Like you can't have one without the other.
So if you're not doing it safely,
then they won't do it at scale.
But ultimately for the
payoffs to be there,
it needs to be a scalable
solution that's employed.
- So safety is a filter,
scale is the proof point?
- Correct.
- So how do you do it at scale?
- So ultimately what we do is,
we've now developed something called
the industrial automation hub.
And what that allows us
to do is, the unique thing
that hasn't been conceptualized before
is that we're able to take AI agents,
the agentic agent infrastructure,
pull in realtime data into that
and then build binaries through AI
that are still pulled safely across
to the client's environment.
But ultimately, it's this
industrial automation hub
that does all the
testing, all the training,
it's your safe sandbox that
you're able to do that in scale.
- And what does scale
mean for your customers?
Is it a single pipe?
How do you even imagine the
concept of scale with midstream?
- So with the power cost
problems that we have nowadays,
power being extremely expensive,
a client might come in and they say,
hey, we want to solve
our power cost issues
at scale across all of our infrastructure,
all the pipelines we have.
Another client might say,
hey, we have a portioned
or prorated lines,
so we don't think we can
actually contractually
get more through the systems.
Well, with automation
and with our technology,
you actually can.
So that's what they want
to do is they want to scale
the solution to the
problem that they have.
- So you're already going
after the mission critical
component of their business.
Like you are impacting
the core of what they do.
- Correct, 100%.
So at the end of the day,
what we're looking to do
is we're not looking to replace the human
or the person that's in that hot seat
day in and day out--
- The operator.
- -12 hours a day.
We're looking to augment them.
So it's very similar to, you know,
instead of using an
abacus, we now have Excel.
Your pilots and planes now have autopilot.
- Your tooling is getting better.
- Exactly.
- Okay, but one another thing
that I would wonder about is,
can you do this without
replacing the existing systems?
Like there's already infrastructure,
there's automation,
there's a SCADA sitting
on that system working.
Can you do this without
touching those systems,
without replacing them?
- Yes.
So everything that we do
is we're SCADA agnostic,
whichever provider you happen to have,
we've architected it that way.
We plug in right alongside
that existing SCADA system,
all of the existing field equipment,
their PLCs, all of that.
We know that it's a lot
of frankenpipe out there,
which means that you have
basically old pipe systems,
new pipe systems are all
merged and acquired together.
Our system needs to be able to orchestrate
and control all that without
there having to be a big lift
and shift in order to do that control.
- So give me more about it
because I'm still skeptical.
There's a lot of data flowing
through the infrastructure,
data being collected, gathered, analyzed,
they're probably running multiple
data collection mechanisms.
It's a lot of complexity there.
How do you come on top of this
and not mess this thing up?
- So, very similar to like
an app on your phone, right?
So an app interfaces with all of that data
that's coming into your phone
for whatever those data sources are.
Ultimately what that
app's purpose is to do
is whatever the problem is
that you're having to solve it.
So similarly for us, whether
you have leak detection,
you might have all sorts of
other data from the field,
safety security alerts, we
ingest all that through SCADA
so that we can take and make real time
executive decisions based off it.
- Okay, can I open it a little bit?
Like what's inside the box?
Is it a set of LLMs, some unique
proprietary context that you give it?
Like how does it work?
- So what we did for
midstream specifically
is we took a solution that's
already been solved downstream.
So APC, Advanced Process
Control, we ported that,
we patent it and ported it across into
one of the tools within our toolbox.
The way APC works is basically,
you can think of it as like a car
once you get it up to speed,
you're in fourth gear,
fifth gear, whatever,
it's a manual car, get it up to speed,
APC will allow you to adjust
the RPMs within any gear.
The issue is that in pipeline space,
or even downstream upstream,
there's a lot of transients that go on.
So a lot of starting and
stopping of the pumps,
the pipes, et cetera.
That's the same as changing
a gear in your car.
What we've done is we've
found a solution in a way
that we are now patenting that
does the discrete control.
So it marries with the APC to do
the transient or the discrete control
in order to orchestrate
optimization results in real time.
- So very unique, very unique intelligence
that you had to put on top of the data.
You have to understand the framework,
the pipelines, the data coming out of it,
contextualize the data.
- Correct.
- Have you done all those steps yourself
or are you using other
pieces of context solutions
and logic from the ecosystem?
- So we don't want to redevelop
and redo the wheel, so to say.
So there's a lot of other solutions
that are out there in terms of like,
in the case of Microsoft, we
leverage like their Azure,
not only their Azure cloud
but some of their ingestion LLMs and such,
in order to really pull that data in,
cleanse the data, QC it
before it can get pulled
and facilitate into our system.
So there's also connectors
when it comes to
the data connectivity
between SCADA and our system.
So we could do that
or we could use an off the shelf solution,
which is what we do.
- And when you go and talk to customers,
how do they take and
interact with your solution
and with the way you are framing it
in context of their business?
What's their reaction to it?
- So initially, I'd say
a couple years back,
it was very much disbelief.
It's like, no, you can't do
this, we can't close the loop.
It's impossible.
We've tried it for the last 20 years.
We've now gotten over
that hump, thankfully,
and now it's a matter of,
okay, we have this problem set
that we want to solve across
these different pipelines,
how fast can you do it?
How fast can you do it safely?
And more importantly,
what's the end operator experience
going to be for those folks?
They're very, very sensitive
to MOC, Management of Change.
And what that means is
that, just like any of us,
when we get into a new car
or when we first learn to ride a bike,
it took some time for us to
become acquainted with it.
So they're super keen on,
they want as little change as possible
for their end community,
their end operators,
so that they can actually get up to speed
using the tool quickly.
- Is it a business decision for them
or a technical decision for them?
Like how do they evaluate it?
- It's both.
So, there's definitely the
business problem that we solve.
So whether that be increasing throughput,
reducing the energy costs,
but ultimately it needs to go through
the technical due diligence of
how is this going to pass our
cybersecurity risk matrix,
how is this going to be
architected and plugged in?
Does this meet baseline requirements
for hardware specs, et cetera?
So it's both sides definitely
have to come together.
- And then there's this
idea of the OT technologies
and IT technologies, SCADA,
you're clearly sitting on the OT side,
where you are bringing this overlay
that looks very much more like IT.
Are you able to match
these two worlds together
with how you approach it?
- That definitely the,
I'd say the paradigm shift
that one of the many paradigm shifts
that our company has
brought to the forefront.
So with IT and OT, the
marrying of those two,
we know very well the OT space,
we also know very well the IT space,
to have them both come together
and to have a closed
loop solution like this,
that relies on the safety and
the orchestration on one side
and the compliance and the
technical bend on the other,
that's really the proverbial
needle that we have to thread.
- And then I would think that, you know,
you bringing the inner loop,
the efficiency of the system itself,
but you also bring in the outer loop,
that's where the IT comes
in, the scale comes in play.
- Yes.
- That's interesting.
But you also have people
involved in the process.
You have the operators.
I would assume with very
unique set of skills
and very difficult to
find somebody who's able
to run an operating room in a pipeline.
- It is.
So a lot of what the industry's facing,
especially in the last decade or so,
is it's that attrition
that continues to happen
as folks are getting older
and they're retiring.
So a lot of that historic
baseline knowledge
that people have developed over decades,
that's leaving the industry.
So having a solution
like ours that comes in
and autonomously is able to
do the closed loop control
while also overlaying
some of that important
historical knowledge from these folks
that are leaving is the perfect coupling
of helping bridge that gap.
- You must be interacting
with a lot of operators.
So you see their reactions.
How do they feel about solutions
that you bring to them?
- So initially the
operators are quite guarded.
There's this, I'd say innate fear,
just like with a lot of AI
technologies out there right now,
that this is going to take my job.
Ultimately what we say
is that, regulatorily,
just like airplanes have
had autopilot for decades,
this is a solution that
really helps the pilot
get up to speed faster
as well as helps them
so that they're not so
exhausted but regulatorily,
they're not going away.
Like, when's the last time any of us
have gotten to an aircraft
without a pilot at the helm?
- That's a great analogy
because yes, you're basically providing
an autopilot to a pilot.
The pilot is still the most
important person on the plane,
but doesn't mean that you will give them
the tools to do their job better.
I really like that framing.
- Yeah, exactly.
- It's fascinating.
What's next for you?
- So we've really put a lot of effort
into our industrial automation hub,
what that's going to allow us
is to unlock the capability to take
and through agentic ai,
facilitate the creation
of these binaries or
basically these solutions
for not just midstream oil and gas,
but additional parts of oil and gas
and then the greater ecosystem as a whole.
We have aspirations of
building out beyond oil and gas
because ultimately at the end of the day,
this architecture is
allowing us to test faster,
give clients the critical
insights that they need
and get to the scale that they need
more efficiently and quickly.
- Yeah, I love it.
It's a really good combination
of bringing the inner loop, the automation
and the outer loop, the
scale into the industry.
Good luck.
I wish you and the company the
best and thank you so much.
- Yeah, thank you.
(upbeat music)
